analysis.one_liner: Requires more paid influencers to register as lobbyists and disclose their work to the public.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would expand who must register as a lobbyist, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee since January 2026 with no hearing, no vote, and 5 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law only requires people to register as lobbyists if lobbying is a big part of their job and if they personally make lobbying contacts. This bill would make paid consultants who advise or steer lobbying contacts register as lobbyists too, and it would cut the time threshold for registration from 20% of a person's paid work to 10%. The result: more of the paid influence trade would be visible to the public in official disclosure records.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens and journalists who rely on lobbying disclosures to see who is trying to shape laws; public interest groups that track influence in Congress; and ethics enforcers, who would gain a fuller registry covering strategic consultants who currently stay off the books.

how_it_helps.text: The bill rewrites the definition of lobbying activity so that paid 'counseling in support of' preparation and planning for lobbying counts as lobbying, not just the personal contacts lobbyists make [S2].

It adds a rule that anyone paid to provide counseling who has the authority to direct or substantially influence a lobbying contact, and who knows the contact was made, is treated as having made that same lobbying contact — pulling behind-the-scenes strategists into the disclosure system [S2].

It lowers the registration threshold from spending less than 20 percent of paid time on lobbying to less than 10 percent, so people whose lobbying work falls between those lines would have to register and file reports [S2].
The changes apply to lobbying contacts made on or after enactment, so the wider registry would take effect immediately for new influence campaigns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms, law firms, and consulting shops whose strategic advice currently falls outside the registration system would take on registration and quarterly reporting duties, and their corporate and trade-association clients would see more of their influence spending become public.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: thousands of advisers, law firms, and consultants who never considered themselves lobbyists would need to register and file quarterly reports, a real burden for small shops [S2].

The bill's standard for who counts — anyone who can 'direct or substantially influence' a lobbying contact and provides paid counseling — is broad, and critics could argue it sweeps in lawyers, strategists, and employees who give incidental advice rather than classic lobbyists [S2].
Disclosure alone does not change the underlying influence: registered lobbyists can still meet lawmakers and shape legislation; the bill makes the activity visible but does not restrict it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but modest: more of the paid influence industry would show up in public lobbying records, which helps voters and journalists follow who is working the halls. The costs fall on lobbying and consulting firms in the form of registration and reporting, and the broad definitions could catch some people who give incidental advice. On balance the bill is a transparency improvement, though it changes disclosure rather than limiting lobbying itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote; with the 119th Congress still in session, it is waiting and moving nowhere.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the bill on January 22, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S4].
Five House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the record shows no action after the committee referral [S3][S4].

The bill would amend the Lobbying Disclosure Act of 1995 to cover paid strategic counseling that supports lobbying and to lower the registration threshold from 20 percent to 10 percent of paid time [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms and strategic consultants who profit from staying outside the registration system, since their work remains undisclosed; no one else gained from the bill stalling.

for.name: Rep. Delia C. Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: 5 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the original cosponsors named at introduction (Williams of Georgia, Mullin, and Simon).

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 22, 2026 and has taken no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill stalled.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor on record is a House Democrat (6 total, all from the 217-member Democratic caucus), with no Republican support in the record.

industries.note: The bill would force more of these firms' strategists and part-time lobbyists to register and file public reports, ending a common way to influence policy without appearing in the disclosure database. Their interest in staying off the registry runs against the public's interest in knowing who is paid to shape laws.

industries.industry: Law firms and strategic consulting practices
industries.note: Advisers paid to counsel lobbying campaigns would be treated as making the lobbying contacts they steer, which brings new registration duties and public exposure for firms that currently advise without registering; some of that advice may be genuinely unrelated to direct lobbying.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade associations that hire lobbyists
industries.note: Their outside consultants would appear in lobbying disclosures, reducing the ability to work influential channels quietly; the underlying ability to lobby would remain unchanged.

analysis.trajectory: With a referral to Judiciary, only 5 cosponsors, and no committee action in the first months after introduction, this bill follows the pattern of most ethics and disclosure bills: it will likely die at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or a vote unless it picks up bipartisan support or an unlikely push from leadership.
